doxycycline.name: Doxycycline
doxycycline.summary: Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic, available on prescription, that is used to treat or prevent certain bacterial infections and to treat rosacea. The NHS says its most common side effects are headaches and feeling or being sick, that it can make skin sensitive to the sun, and that it is not usually used during pregnancy or breastfeeding because it can affect a baby's teeth.
usedFor: Chest infections, dental infections and skin infections caused by bacteria
Sexually transmitted infections and some rarer infections
Acne, where MedlinePlus says it acts on bacteria in the pores and reduces skin oil
Prevention of malaria in people travelling abroad

For rosacea, MedlinePlus describes a different effect, a reduction in inflammation of the skin. Like other antibiotics, it does not work against viral infections such as colds and flu.

Rare effects listed by the NHS include inflammation of the bowel, changes in blood cells, liver problems, pancreatitis and raised pressure around the brain; new or worrying symptoms are a reason for a GP appointment, or NHS 111 if urgent

Antacids, iron, zinc, calcium and magnesium can reduce how well doxycycline is absorbed, and leaflets differ on how far apart to space them
UK product information says isotretinoin and other systemic retinoids are best avoided with doxycycline, as each has been linked to raised pressure around the brain
The NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol with doxycycline because it can stop it working properly
The NHS says doxycycline does not stop contraception working, but being sick or severe diarrhoea for more than 24 hours may reduce the protection of contraceptive pills
doxycycline.monitoring: For rosacea the NHS says a doctor usually reviews progress after some weeks. With warfarin, product information reports a longer prothrombin time, and a Scottish pharmacy direction describes a clotting (INR) check after starting the antibiotic.

sections.heading: What is doxycycline used for?
sections.body:
Doxycycline is an antibiotic, a medicine that treats or prevents certain infections caused by bacteria. In the UK it is available only with a prescription. The NHS lists chest infections, dental infections and skin infections among the problems it treats, together with rosacea, sexually transmitted infections and some rarer infections. It can also be used to prevent malaria in people travelling abroad, and people taking it for that reason are not expected to feel any different.

MedlinePlus adds that it is used for acne, where it acts on the bacteria in the pores and lowers the amount of oil on the skin. Like other antibiotics, it does not work against viral infections such as colds and flu.

sections.heading: How does doxycycline work and how is it taken?
sections.body:
Doxycycline belongs to the tetracycline group of antibiotics. The NHS explains that it stops bacteria from making the proteins they need to survive. In rosacea, MedlinePlus describes a different benefit, a reduction in inflammation of the skin. With most infections people usually start to feel better within a few days, while rosacea responds more slowly and is normally reviewed by a doctor after some weeks.

Doxycycline comes as capsules, tablets and dispersible tablets, which are dissolved in water before they are taken. The NHS describes swallowing capsules and standard tablets whole with water and staying upright for a while afterwards. For some strengths, taking it with food makes feeling sick less likely. The NHS stresses that finishing the whole course matters, even when symptoms have eased.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of doxycycline?
sections.body:
The NHS says the most common side effects are headaches and feeling or being sick. Doxycycline can also make the skin sensitive to the sun. Pharmacy guidance describes avoiding direct sunlight and ultraviolet light, including sunbeds and sun lamps, and covering up, wearing a hat and sunglasses and using sunscreen when exposure cannot be avoided. A fingernail that starts to come away from its base is listed among the serious effects and is linked to a reaction to sunlight.

The NHS lists pain or difficulty swallowing, a sore throat, acid reflux, reduced appetite and chest pain that worsens with eating as possible signs of an inflamed or ulcerated food pipe. These are reasons to contact the GP, or NHS 111 if symptoms are marked. Serious allergic reactions are rare, and the NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell or breathing becomes difficult. Other rare effects include inflammation of the bowel, changes in blood cells, liver problems, pancreatitis and raised pressure around the brain.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with doxycycline?
sections.body: The NHS says doxycycline is usually taken by adults and older children, and that younger children can take it for some infections. A previous allergic reaction to doxycycline or another medicine, kidney or liver problems, lupus and myasthenia gravis are listed as reasons it may not be suitable. It is not usually used during pregnancy because it can affect how a baby's teeth develop. It is also not usually used while breastfeeding, because of a risk of side effects in the baby or effects on the baby's teeth. UK product information is stricter and lists pregnancy and breastfeeding as contraindications. The NHS says doxycycline does not stop any type of contraception from working, but being sick or severe diarrhoea for more than 24 hours may reduce the protection of contraceptive pills.

sections.heading: Doxycycline with other medicines and alcohol
sections.body: The NHS says anticoagulants such as warfarin, antacids, acne medicines, and iron or zinc supplements may not mix well with doxycycline. Antacids, iron, zinc, calcium and magnesium can reduce how much doxycycline is absorbed, and leaflets differ on how far apart they should be spaced. UK product information says isotretinoin and other systemic retinoids are best avoided with doxycycline, because each has been linked to raised pressure around the brain. With warfarin, product information reports a longer prothrombin time, a measure of how quickly blood clots, and says lower anticoagulant doses may be needed. The NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol with doxycycline because it can stop it working properly. Apart from alcohol, the NHS says people can eat and drink normally while taking it.

faqs.q: Does doxycycline stop contraception from working?
faqs.a: The NHS says doxycycline does not stop any type of contraception from working, including the combined pill, the progestogen-only pill and emergency contraception. The exception is being sick or having severe diarrhoea for more than 24 hours, which may mean contraceptive pills do not protect against pregnancy.

faqs.q: Can people drink alcohol while taking doxycycline?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol with doxycycline, because alcohol can stop it working properly. Apart from that, it says people can eat and drink normally while taking it.

faqs.q: Does doxycycline make skin more sensitive to the sun?
faqs.a: Yes, the NHS says doxycycline can make the skin sensitive to the sun. Pharmacy guidance describes avoiding direct sunlight and sunbeds, and covering up and using sunscreen when exposure cannot be avoided.

faqs.q: Is doxycycline used during pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is not usually used during pregnancy because it can affect how a baby's teeth develop. It is also not usually used while breastfeeding, because of a risk of side effects in the baby or effects on their teeth.

faqs.q: How quickly does doxycycline start to work?
faqs.a: For most infections the NHS says people usually feel better within a few days, though the full course still matters. Rosacea responds more slowly and is usually reviewed by a doctor after some weeks, and people taking it to prevent malaria are not expected to feel any different.

faqs.q: Will doxycycline work for a cold or flu?
faqs.a: No, the NHS says antibiotics such as doxycycline do not work for colds, flu or other viral infections. They are used for infections caused by bacteria.

tetracyclines.name: Tetracyclines
tetracyclines.summary: Tetracyclines are a group of antibiotics that stop bacteria from making the proteins they need to survive. Doxycycline is the member described here, and the NHS lists it for chest, dental and skin infections, rosacea and some sexually transmitted infections.
